Pregnancy

Pregnancy nausea: food, fluids, medicines and when to seek help

Updated: October 11, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Pregnancy nausea can happen all day and can disrupt eating, work and rest. Small changes may help mild symptoms, but you do not have to endure severe sickness or wait for dehydration before asking for treatment.

When pregnancy sickness happens

Nausea often starts around weeks 4–7, may peak near week 9 and usually improves by weeks 16–20. Some people have symptoms for longer; others never feel sick. Its presence or absence does not reliably measure the health or sex of a baby.

Vomiting that first starts after 16 weeks, or comes with abdominal pain, fever or urinary symptoms, needs assessment for other causes. Infection, gastrointestinal illness and other pregnancy conditions should not automatically be labelled morning sickness.

Hormones, susceptibility and triggers

Research supports an important role for GDF15, produced largely by the fetal–placental unit, and the pregnant person’s sensitivity to it. Genetics and exposure before pregnancy help explain differences in severity. This is not a failure of willpower, and experimental hormone-based approaches are not home treatments.

Previous pregnancy sickness, twins or more, family history, migraine or motion sickness can increase susceptibility. Tiredness, an empty stomach, smells or travel may worsen symptoms. Skin colour is not a useful personal prediction, and nausea cannot tell you whether a baby is a girl. No single risk factor determines your experience.

Recognising hyperemesis gravidarum

Hyperemesis gravidarum (HG) is severe pregnancy sickness that prevents normal eating or drinking and substantially limits daily life. Estimates vary, commonly around 1–3 in 100 pregnancies. You can need treatment before major weight loss or abnormal tests develop.

Persistent sickness can cause dehydration, low urine output, weight loss, nutritional or electrolyte problems, weakness, dizziness and a racing pulse. Mild-to-moderate sickness usually does not harm the baby; severe ongoing illness may affect growth and needs follow-up. Emotional distress also deserves support. Abdominal pain requires assessment rather than being assumed to be HG.

Small, tolerable meals

Try small meals or snacks rather than three large portions. Plain crackers, dry toast, rice, pasta or cereal may be easier to manage; a bedside snack before getting up helps some people. Avoid long gaps if an empty stomach worsens symptoms, and eat slowly.

Include protein-containing foods you tolerate, such as yoghurt or well-cooked eggs, alongside other foods. Cold meals may smell less. Reduce rich, greasy or spicy foods only if they trigger you; there is no compulsory menu. Follow pregnancy food-safety guidance, and ask for dietary help if your intake stays restricted.

Fluids, rest and practical comfort

Sip tolerable drinks little and often rather than forcing a large glass. Some people prefer fluids between meals, but a universal thirty-minute separation is unnecessary: keeping fluids down matters more. If you cannot drink enough, do not rely on crackers or water alone to treat dehydration.

Rest and help with meals, childcare or work can reduce strain. Fresh air and ventilation may ease odour triggers; gentle movement is optional when you feel well enough. Sleep or slow breathing can be comforting but does not cure HG. Avoid smoking and second-hand smoke, and ask others to keep your space smoke-free.

Supplements, screens and complementary options

If a prenatal supplement worsens nausea, ask about changing its timing, formulation or iron component. Bedtime is not best for everyone. Keep essential supplements such as prescribed folic acid on an agreed plan; do not stop essential medicines yourself. Take breaks or adjust screen brightness and text size if scrolling or visual strain triggers symptoms.

Ginger-containing foods or drinks may help mild-to-moderate nausea; ask a pharmacist before concentrated supplements. Wrist acupressure may be an additional option. Lemon scent may feel pleasant to some people, but it is not a proven miracle cure, and evidence for aromatherapy is limited. Avoid ingesting essential oils or using unreviewed remedies instead of treatment.

Medicines can be offered early

Contact your maternity clinician or doctor when symptoms interfere with eating, drinking or daily activities. Pregnancy-appropriate anti-sickness medicines include selected antihistamines or doxylamine with pyridoxine; other medicines may be used if these do not work. Availability and the best choice vary, so discuss benefits, side effects and your previous responses rather than self-prescribing.

Metoclopramide or ondansetron may be considered when needed; each has specific risks to discuss, including a very small possible increase in oral clefts with early ondansetron exposure. The risks of untreated severe sickness matter too. If tablets will not stay down, a clinician can arrange another route. Do not increase doses or combine remedies without advice.

Assessment, day care and hospital treatment

The team asks about intake, urine, weight, symptoms, medicines and daily functioning, and may check vital signs, blood or urine and arrange a scan where indicated. Urine ketones alone do not measure dehydration or determine how ill you are. Treatment can include antiemetics, intravenous fluids and correction of electrolyte problems.

Some people improve with outpatient or day-care treatment; others need admission because of dehydration, continuing vomiting, abnormal blood results or inability to take essential medicines. With prolonged vomiting or very poor intake, clinicians provide thiamine (vitamin B1), particularly before intravenous glucose or artificial nutrition, to prevent serious deficiency. Ongoing severe illness may need nutrition, clot-risk and fetal-growth review.

When to get urgent help

Seek prompt same-day clinical advice if you cannot keep drinks or essential medicines down, are losing weight, have very dark or scant urine, feel weak or dizzy, or have fever, abdominal pain or blood in vomit. No urine for more than 8 hours or inability to retain food or fluids for 24 hours are concerning signs; do not wait for those times if you are worsening.

Call emergency services for fainting or loss of consciousness, confusion, severe breathing difficulty, chest pain, severe abdominal pain or substantial bleeding. Blood in vomit with feeling unwell, faintness, abdominal pain or abnormal breathing also needs emergency care. Vomiting with severe headache, vision changes or pain under the ribs later in pregnancy needs immediate maternity assessment. After treatment, follow the medication and review plan; if sickness or dehydration returns, seek reassessment rather than waiting for a routine appointment.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Early assessment and individual antiemetic choices can prevent avoidable deterioration.

Severe pregnancy sickness does not automatically require admission, but home remedies do not replace medical treatment.

Hydration, nutrition and mental wellbeing all matter; no symptom or risk factor predicts an individual outcome.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help you record sickness, drinks you tolerate and questions for appointments. It cannot assess dehydration, diagnose HG or choose a medicine; concerning symptoms take priority over app records.

When to seek help

Seek prompt care for persistent vomiting or dehydration signs. Fainting or loss of consciousness, confusion, severe pain, chest pain, severe breathing difficulty or substantial bleeding require emergency help. Do not delay care to try another food or remedy.

Evidence notes updated: October 11, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Pregnancy sickness can occur at any time; new vomiting after 16 weeks needs consideration of other causes.
  • Small meals, tolerable fluids and trigger adjustments may help, but they do not replace treatment for severe sickness.
  • HG can be treated in the community, day care or hospital according to clinical need; early medicines may help.
  • Poor intake, dehydration signs, pain, fever or bleeding need prompt care; fainting or loss of consciousness or severe symptoms need emergency help.

Frequently asked questions

What causes pregnancy nausea?

GDF15 from the fetal–placental unit and individual sensitivity play an important role. Previous sickness, multiple pregnancy and other factors can increase susceptibility. Skin colour is not a useful personal predictor of pregnancy sickness. Nausea does not reliably predict a baby’s sex.

What complications can severe sickness cause?

Dehydration, weight loss, electrolyte or vitamin deficiency and major disruption of daily life can occur. Severe ongoing illness may affect fetal growth. Do not wait for a particular amount of weight loss before seeking help.

What can I eat when I feel sick?

Try small, frequent portions of tolerable foods such as crackers, toast or rice, with protein foods as tolerated. Cold food may be easier. Ask for treatment and dietary help if you cannot eat or drink adequately.

Does ginger or lemon cure pregnancy sickness?

Ginger may help milder symptoms, but supplements need advice. Lemon scent is not a proven cure. Neither should delay anti-sickness medicine or assessment for dehydration.

Must everyone with HG stay in hospital?

No. Some people improve with medicines and day-care fluids; others need admission for ongoing vomiting, dehydration, abnormal tests or other medical risks. The team decides with you based on your condition.

Can I take anti-sickness medicine early in pregnancy?

Clinicians can offer suitable medicines, including in early pregnancy. The choice depends on benefits, specific risks and your history; untreated severe sickness also has risks. Do not self-prescribe or stop essential medicines.

Must I avoid drinking with meals or take every vitamin at night?

No universal schedule suits everyone. Choose tolerable fluid timing and ask about supplement timing or formulation. Maintaining hydration and an agreed essential supplement plan is more important than rigid rules.

When should I call for help?

Seek prompt advice for poor fluid intake, scant dark urine, dizziness, weight loss, fever, pain or blood in vomit. Fainting or loss of consciousness, confusion, severe pain, chest pain, severe breathlessness or substantial bleeding require emergency care.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
